newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rebel sees continued Australia/NZ focus.
newsitem.headline: Rebel sees continued Australia/NZ focus.

text.p: Rebel Sport Ltd joint managing director Ian Dresner said the sporting goods retailer would continue its focus on Australia and New Zealand despite the sale of a strategic stake to the Goh brothers of Singapore.
Dresner said on Wednesday that the company expected to have about 45 superstores in Australia by the year 2000 compared with 23 currently.

"We are looking about doubling our turnover in the next two to three years," he told Reuters after a news conference to announce that the Goh brothers had acquired a 19.9 percent stake from two founding shareholders at a cost of A$12.7 million.

The Goh brothers, who own the World of Sports Holdings Pte Ltd sporting goods retail chain and control Singapore-listed sporting goods, apparel and property group Ossia International Ltd, paid A$1.65 per share for the holding which was sold by Rebel chairman Sam Linz and director Robert Gavshon.
Dresner and fellow managing director Hilton Seskin acquired another eight percent stake from Linz and Gavshon, lifting their combined holding to 18 percent.
Dresner said Rebel this calendar year planned to open four superstores in Australia and another four in New Zealand, where it already had three stores.
Dresner said he would not comment on the company's immediate financial outlook as the 1996/97 (April-March) profit result was due to be released next week.
The company achieved an after-tax profit of A$3.09 million last year on sales of A$114.95 million.
World of Sports chairman George Goh said there were synergies between the two companies.
"Rebel has created trends in sporting goods retail rather than followed them and its outstanding management, unique marketing blend and potential for growth echoes that of our own company," Goh said.
Goh said World of Sports, which has more 50 stores in Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei, Indonesia, and Taiwan, was looking to expand into China as well.
Rebel shares, which rose five cents when the Goh deal was announced mid-morning, were steady at A$1.65 at 1.30 p.m. (0330 GMT).
Dresner said he hoped the Goh investment would be a positive for the share price which had been under pressure due to the six months of speculation about what would happen to the 28 percent stake.
